blindSummary:
This country is comparatively safe for trans visitors, with a cleaner documented traveler-axis profile than its neighbours: no mob violence, trans-tourist rape, police-brutality case, or foreign-trans-detention case surfaced in research. The coastal tourist regions have a long international-tourism culture and are broadly open, and the capital has the most established gay scene in the surrounding region.

The framework is weaker than in the most protective neighbouring countries: legal gender recognition (available since 2015) is partial and not self-ID (it covers only some documents), there is no marriage equality (a 2013 constitutional ban), and an anti-gender movement is active. A 2024 prosecution of an accommodation host who refused to take a gay couple shows enforcement works, and the head of state was formally criticised for outing a minister.

The conservative religious climate is more marked outside the main tourist areas. The country belongs to a regional bloc and its border-free travel area, so border friction for most travellers is low.
blindOutOfScope: General tourist-season crime and border checks for foreign nationals affect all travellers.
blindSourceSummaries: The capital's Pride organisation's documentation report (2018) on this country's implementation of a regional human-rights body's recommendation on the rights of LGBTI persons: hate-crime legislation and under-reporting of homophobic/transphobic crimes, hate-speech case studies, freedom of assembly, legal gender recognition, same-sex partnership recognition, employment discrimination, and compiled hate-crime data with case studies.

A regional LGBTI-rights organisation's annual review 2025 (covering 2024), chapter on this country: a prosecutor in a coastal city charged a man for refusing a gay couple's accommodation booking (2018 incident); anti-gender disinformation escalating - a parliamentary session on 'gender ideology' featured speakers spreading misinformation with no LGBTI organisations invited; the first Pride march in another coastal city faced disruption the day before.
Legal-journal article (2026): academic analysis of the specific characteristics of conducting personal searches of transgender, trans and gender non-conforming persons under this country's law.
A foreign government's archived 2021 human-rights-practices report on this country: official assessment including treatment of LGBTI persons.

Encyclopedia overview: same-sex activity legal since 1977; life partnership since 2014; gender identity and expression sections; hate-crime legislation; police cooperation; Pride events in the capital and several other cities plus a regional trans and intersex march; LGBT tourism.

A travel company's country guide: LGBTQIA+ travellers are widely accepted; same-sex relations have been legal for decades and recent laws extend life partnership and protections, but affection in public can draw unwelcome responses in smaller towns and queer venues barely exist outside the capital.

Legal experts' country report for a regional bloc's executive on non-discrimination in this country (2024, reporting period 2023): adoption and implementation of the bloc's equality directives, including on SOGI grounds.

Local LGBT news site (May 2014): the country's second-largest city got an LGBT centre - the second in this country and the first in its coastal region; the city's 4th Pride march (7 June 2014) was announced with the slogan 'full equality', repeated from the previous year to signal LGBT people's unequal position here.

Local LGBT news site (Oct 2014): a new LGBTIQ+ centre was presented in a port city - founded from the local community's need for more active LGBTIQ+ development in the surrounding region, networking with national and international organisations.
blindLocalsOnly: The partial, non-self-ID legal-gender-recognition regime (since 2015, covering only some documents) is resident-facing.
